lead: A TRIAC conducts in both directions, so one TRIAC replaces the antiparallel SCR pair of an AC voltage controller and needs only one gate circuit. Delaying its turn-on in each half cycle cuts away the start of every half wave, and the RMS voltage at the load falls smoothly. Lamp dimmers and fan regulators use it. The exam asks how the gate is fired with positive and negative pulses, and how the RC-DIAC network sets the firing angle.
prereq: You need: the full-wave AC voltage controller and its RMS formula from AC voltage controllers: phase and on-off control, and the TRIAC and DIAC devices from power semiconductor devices.

sections.h3: The TRIAC as an AC switch

blocks.text: A TRIAC has two main terminals, MT1 and MT2, and a gate G. MT1 is the reference: gate voltage and gate current are always measured from MT1. It behaves as two antiparallel SCRs sharing one gate.

items: Latching current IL: the current that must flow as the gate pulse ends for the TRIAC to stay on.
Holding current IH: the current below which a conducting TRIAC turns off. It is smaller than IL; the TRIAC turns off at every current zero.

blocks.text: A TRIAC must block the reverse voltage at once after turning off, whereas each SCR of a pair gets a half cycle to recover. With a fan the voltage jumps across the TRIAC at the current zero, and this commutating dv/dt can turn it straight back on, so fan regulators carry a snubber.

sections.h3: Triggering quadrants: positive and negative gate pulses

blocks.text: A triggering quadrant is one combination of MT2 polarity and gate-current polarity, both measured from MT1. A typical data sheet asks for about twice as much gate current in Q4 as in the other three, and three-quadrant TRIACs are not rated for Q4 at all.
A dimmer fires the TRIAC once with MT2 positive and once with MT2 negative, so the pulse polarity decides which two quadrants it uses.

items: Positive pulses only: Q1 in the positive half and Q4 in the negative half. The negative half may fire late or not at all, giving a DC component. Avoid it.
Negative pulses only: Q2 and Q3. The usual drive from a microcontroller: the gate is simply pulled below MT1.
Pulse polarity following MT2: Q1 and Q3. A DIAC does this by itself.

sections.h3: The RC-DIAC dimmer and its firing angle

blocks.text: The lamp is in series with the TRIAC. A resistor R (potentiometer plus fixed resistor) and a capacitor C sit across the TRIAC, and a DIAC joins C to the gate. While the TRIAC is off, the capacitor voltage v<sub>C</sub> is a sine that lags the supply by tan⁻¹(ωRC). When |v<sub>C</sub>| reaches the DIAC breakover voltage V<sub>BO</sub>, about 30 V, the DIAC snaps on and dumps the charge of C into the gate as one sharp pulse.

α ≈ tan⁻¹(ωRC) + sin⁻¹(VBO/VCm). The first term is the lag of vC; the second is how far vC must rise past its zero to reach VBO. Its peak is VCm = √2 VsXC/√(R² + XC²), with XC = 1/(ωC). This ignores the loading by the gate, which is fine for an estimate.

The DIAC is symmetrical, so its pulse has the polarity of v<sub>C</sub>, which follows MT2: Q1 and Q3. Raising R makes v<sub>C</sub> lag more and shrink, so α grows. One RC stage cannot delay much beyond 120° to 150°, so dimmers that must go fully dark add a second stage.

From a microcontroller, an optotriac gives isolated drive: a random-phase type for phase control, a zero-crossing type for on-off control of heaters. A series RC snubber across MT1 and MT2 limits dv/dt; 100 Ω with 0.1 µF is a common starting point.

examples.question: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 230 V, 100 W incandescent lamp through a TRIAC dimmer fired at α = 90° in both half cycles. Take the lamp resistance as its rated hot value. Find the lamp resistance, the RMS lamp voltage, the RMS current and the lamp power.
steps: Lamp resistance at rated conditions: R = V²/P = 230²/100 = 52 900/100 = 529 Ω.
examples.answer: R = 529 Ω, V<sub>o</sub> = 162.6 V, I<sub>o</sub> = 0.307 A, P = 50.0 W, half the rated power. A real filament runs cooler, so it takes a little more than 50 W, and its light falls by much more than half.

examples.question: The dimmer's trigger network has R = 100 kΩ and C = 0.1 µF across the TRIAC, and a DIAC with V<sub>BO</sub> = 30 V. Estimate the firing angle. What is it when the potentiometer is turned down so that R = 10 kΩ?
steps: Lag of v<sub>C</sub>: tan⁻¹(R/X<sub>C</sub>) = tan⁻¹(100/31.83) = tan⁻¹(3.142) = 72.3°.
v<sub>C</sub> reaches 30 V at sin⁻¹(30/98.7) = 17.7° past its own zero, so α = 72.3° + 17.7° = 90.0°. This is the 90° of the first example.
examples.answer: α ≈ 90° at 100 kΩ and about 23° at 10 kΩ, where the lamp is nearly at full brightness (V<sub>o</sub> = 228.5 V by the RMS formula).

traps: Naming the quadrant from the gate polarity alone. A positive gate pulse is Q1 when MT2 is positive but Q4 when MT2 is negative.
Writing that a negative-only gate drive cannot fire the positive half cycle. It fires in Q2, which works; it is the positive-only drive that lands in the weak Q4.
Swapping latching and holding current. Latching current must flow as the gate pulse ends; holding current is the level at which a conducting TRIAC drops out, and I<sub>H</sub> < I<sub>L</sub>.
Curing false triggering with a weaker gate drive. The usual cause is a fast dv/dt across MT1 and MT2, and the cure is a snubber.
Assuming one RC stage gives the full 0° to 180° range. In the worked example even 220 kΩ only delays the pulse to about 122°.

quiz.q: Name the terminals of a TRIAC and the terminal the gate is measured from.
quiz.a: MT1, MT2 and the gate G. Gate voltage and current are measured from MT1.

quiz.q: List the four triggering quadrants by MT2 and gate polarity.
quiz.a: Q1: MT2 +, gate +. Q2: MT2 +, gate −. Q3: MT2 −, gate −. Q4: MT2 −, gate +.

quiz.q: Why does an RC-DIAC dimmer fire the TRIAC in Q1 and Q3?
quiz.a: The DIAC breaks over either way, so its pulse has the polarity of the capacitor voltage, which has the polarity of MT2 when the DIAC fires.

quiz.q: Why do microcontroller TRIAC drivers usually use negative gate pulses in both half cycles?
quiz.a: Negative pulses fire in Q2 and Q3 and are easy to make by pulling the gate below MT1. Positive-only pulses would need the weak Q4 in the negative half.

quiz.q: The 529 Ω lamp of the worked example is fired at α = 60° from 230 V. Find V<sub>o</sub> and the power.
In the dimmer of worked example 2 the potentiometer is turned up so that R = 220 kΩ. Estimate α.
A driver gives only positive pulses through a pulse transformer. The lamp flickers and a transformer in the circuit hums. Explain.
quiz.a: In the negative half the pulse lands in Q4, so the TRIAC fires late or not at all. The half cycles differ, the load gets a DC part, and the DC saturates the transformer. Use negative pulses, or reverse them with MT2.

beyond: Not for the exam. Smart dimmers use back-to-back MOSFETs, which can switch off at any instant (trailing-edge dimming) and need no holding current, so they suit LED lamps. TRIAC dimmers for LEDs add a bleeder that keeps the current above I<sub>H</sub>. Search for "TRIAC gate quadrants", "leading and trailing edge dimming" and "snubberless TRIAC".
